summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys Switzerland across history, sport, energy policy, economy, government, demographics, language, religion, environment, neutrality and defence. It traces the country from Burgundian, Alemannic and Frankish rule through the Helvetic Republic and the Act of Mediation, to the 1848 Federal Constitution and later women's suffrage. It also covers the country's wealth, nuclear phaseout plan, multilingual regions, immigration, and its position outside the European Union but inside the Schengen Area.
one_line: Overview of Switzerland's history, politics, economy, society, language, religion and environmental record.
key_facts: Switzerland is officially the Swiss Confederation (Latin: Confoederatio Helvetica) and is a federal directorial republic of 26 cantons, with Bern as the seat of federal authorities.
The Federal Constitution adopted in 1848 is the legal foundation of the modern federal state, and it is among the oldest constitutions in the world.
Switzerland was the last Western republic to grant women the right to vote; the federal level achieved it in 1971, and Appenzell Innerrhoden granted it in 1990.
Elisabeth Kopp was the first woman on the seven-member Federal Council, serving from 1984–1989, and Ruth Dreifuss was the first female president in 1999.
On 25 May 2011 the Swiss government announced plans to end its use of nuclear energy within the next 2 or 3 decades, with the last reactor offline in 2034.
Switzerland was ranked the wealthiest country in the world per capita in 2011, with wealth defined to include both financial and non-financial assets.
The first university in Switzerland was founded in 1460 in Basel, and the University of Zurich is the biggest with nearly 25,000 students.
Christianity is the predominant religion, with the Catholic Church at 38.21% of the population and the Swiss Reformed Church at 26.93% (2000-era figures as given).
In 2012, resident foreigners made up 23.3% of the population, with Italians the largest single group at 15.6% of the foreign population.
Switzerland was the first state to join the United Nations by referendum, becoming a full member in 2002.
Switzerland is not a member of the European Union, but it does participate in the Schengen Area.
In 1803 Napoleon organised a meeting in Paris that produced the Act of Mediation, which restored Swiss autonomy and introduced a Confederation of 19 cantons.
Heidi, by Johanna Spyri (1827–1901), is one of the most popular children's books ever and has become a symbol of Switzerland.
Switzerland has no navy because it is landlocked, but armed military patrol boats are used on lakes bordering neighbouring countries.
Switzerland ratified the Kyoto Protocol in 2003 after signing it in 1998, and the 2014 Global Green Economy Index ranked it among the top 10 green economies.
